section.title: The Golden Lampstand and Two Olive Trees
section.sectionRationale: The fifth night vision, the heart of the eight. Zechariah sees a golden lampstand fed continuously by two olive trees, and hears the word that anchors the whole book: Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit. The vision assures Zerubbabel that he will finish the temple he began, that mountains of opposition will flatten before God's Spirit, and that no one should despise the day of small things.
section.thesis: The LORD's work is accomplished not by human strength but by His Spirit; the same God who fuels the lamp without human effort will level every mountain of opposition and bring Zerubbabel's small beginning to a shouted completion of grace.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the vision of the golden lampstand and two olive trees; the word to Zerubbabel, not by might but by My Spirit, and the leveling of the mountain; and the interpretation of the two olive trees as the two anointed ones.

verses.text: Then the angel who was speaking with me returned and woke me, as a man is awakened from his sleep.
“What do you see?” he asked. “I see a solid gold {{menorah|lampstand}},” I replied, “with a bowl at the top and seven lamps on it, with seven spouts to the lamps.
There are also two olive trees beside it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on its left.”
“What are these, my lord?” I asked the angel who was speaking with me.
“Do you not know what they are?” replied the angel. “No, my lord,” I answered.

units.label: Not by might, but by My Spirit

verses.text: So he said to me, “This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by {{chayil|might}} nor by {{koach|power}}, but by My {{ruach|Spirit}}, says the LORD of Hosts.
What are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you will become a plain. Then he will bring forth the capstone accompanied by shouts of ‘Grace, grace to it!’”
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will complete it. Then you will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent me to you.
For who has despised the day of small things? But these seven eyes of the LORD, which scan the whole earth, will rejoice when they see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel.”
Then I asked the angel, “What are the two olive trees on the right and left of the lampstand?”
And I questioned him further, “What are the two olive branches beside the two gold pipes from which the golden oil pours?”
“Do you not know what these are?” he inquired. “No, my lord,” I replied.
So he said, “These are the two {{yitshar|anointed ones}} who are standing beside the Lord of all the earth.”

menorah.gloss: The lampstand, the golden seven-branched light that stood in the tabernacle and temple, symbol of God's presence and of His people as light-bearers. Here it is fed automatically by two olive trees, needing no priest to trim or refill it, a picture of a work sustained entirely by God's own supply.

chayil.gloss: Might, strength, army, wealth, the collective force of an organized host. It names the kind of power a nation musters to get things done. The vision denies that God's work depends on such human muscle; even organized strength cannot accomplish what only the Spirit can.

koach.gloss: Power, strength, ability, the personal vigor and capacity of an individual. Paired with chayil, it covers strength both corporate and personal. God sets both aside: neither armies nor individual prowess builds His house; His Spirit does.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. The Spirit of God is the divine power by which God creates, empowers, and accomplishes His purposes. By My Spirit is the positive answer to the denial of might and power: the temple, and every work of God, is completed by the Spirit's enabling, not human resources.

yitshar.gloss: Fresh oil, the golden olive oil that fuels the lamp. The two anointed ones are literally the two sons of fresh oil, those saturated with the oil of God's anointing. They stand for the anointed offices of priest and king, Joshua and Zerubbabel, through whom God channels His grace to His people.

basic.context: This is the fifth and central night vision. Zechariah sees a golden lampstand kept burning by two olive trees that feed it oil without any human hand. The meaning comes in the famous word to Zerubbabel, the governor rebuilding the temple: Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit. The mountain of opposition will flatten, the temple will be finished, and no one should look down on its small beginnings.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a symbolic vision with a clear central message. The self-feeding lamp pictures a work God supplies. People debate exactly who the two olive trees or anointed ones are, most likely Joshua the priest and Zerubbabel the governor, but the heart of the passage is unmistakable: God's work is done by God's Spirit.
basic.originalLanguages: The menorah, the golden lampstand, is fed automatically. God says the work is done not by chayil, might or army, nor by koach, personal power, but by His ruach, His Spirit. The two anointed ones are literally the two sons of yitshar, fresh oil, saturated with God's anointing.
basic.typology: The lampstand fed by oil without human effort pictures the church shining by the Spirit's supply, and points to Christ, the true light. The two anointed ones, priest and king, foreshadow Christ, who unites both offices. The rejected capstone crowned with shouts of grace anticipates the stone the builders rejected becoming the chief cornerstone.
basic.christ: The two anointed offices of priest and king, here divided between Joshua and Zerubbabel, are united in Jesus, the true priest-king, the Anointed One filled without measure by the Spirit. The capstone brought forth with shouts of grace points to Christ, the rejected stone made the cornerstone. His whole work, and ours, is accomplished by the Spirit.
basic.god: God accomplishes His purposes by His own Spirit, not by human strength, so that all the glory is His and grace gets the shout. He does not despise small beginnings; His all-seeing eyes rejoice over the smallest faithful start. He supplies His people continually, like oil to a lamp, so their light never depends on their own reserves.
basic.crossReferences: Haggai 2 assures Zerubbabel and the same builders. Psalm 118 and Matthew 21 speak of the rejected stone made the cornerstone. Revelation 11 takes up the two olive trees and lampstands. Ephesians 3 and Acts 1 show God's work done by the Spirit's power.
basic.oneStory: The central vision plants a truth that runs through all of Scripture: God builds His house by His Spirit, not by human might, and He glories in small beginnings crowned by grace. It points to Christ the priest-king and to the church that shines by the Spirit's endless supply, carrying the story toward the finished house of God.

context.literary:
The vision opens with the angel having to wake the prophet 'as a man is awakened from his sleep' (4:1). The night has been long, and this is the fifth vision in a single night. The verb for waking is the root of the call in chapter 2, 'He has roused Himself' (2:13). What follows is the most carefully built of the eight.

The passage is a frame around a centre. Zechariah sees the lampstand and the two trees (verses 2 and 3), and asks what they are. He is told, 'Do you not know?' and answers, 'No, my lord' (verses 4 and 5). Then the explanation is held back, and a word to Zerubbabel is inserted (verses 6 to 10). Only at the end does Zechariah ask about the trees again, receive the same question and give the same answer, and get the interpretation (verses 11 to 14). The identical exchange stands on either side of the central oracle, so that the famous line, 'Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,' sits at the heart of a ring.

The oracle itself is a rhythm of three. Verse 6 is a balanced statement of what the work will not and will depend on. Verse 7 turns to address the mountain directly, in a question that sounds like a taunt, and then ends with shouts. Verses 9 and 10 argue from the past to the future: the hands that laid the foundation will complete the house, and no one should look down on a small beginning.

The vision is paired with the fourth. Joshua the priest was the subject of chapter 3; Zerubbabel the governor is the subject here. And the seven lamps of verse 2 are matched by the 'seven eyes of the LORD' in verse 10, linking the light of the lampstand with the sight of God.
context.historical:
Zerubbabel was of David's line, a descendant of Jeconiah (1 Chronicles 3:17 to 19), and governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1). The line of David had no throne, and the grandson of the last king to be exiled was administering a Persian province. That is the context in which the LORD speaks to him of a work that depends on something other than royal power.

His task was the temple. The foundation had been laid at the first return, and the sight divided the crowd: the people shouted for joy, but many older priests and Levites who had seen the first temple wept so loudly that the sounds could not be told apart (Ezra 3:10 to 13). Then opposition stopped the work for years (Ezra 4:24), until Haggai and Zechariah stirred the leaders in 520 BC (Ezra 5:1 and 5:2). Haggai had put the discouragement into words: 'Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?' (Haggai 2:3). 'The day of small things' in Zechariah 4:10 answers that comparison.

The 'great mountain' is not a particular enemy. The Hebrew word names a barrier, and the obstacles were many: local opposition, Persian bureaucracy, a poor economy, and the weight of grief and comparison. The promise that it would become a plain was met in a way anyone could check. The temple was finished on the third day of Adar in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15), about four years after this night.

Oil was familiar to every hearer. It fuelled the lamps of the tabernacle and temple, and it was the substance with which priests and kings were anointed (Exodus 29:7; 1 Samuel 16:13). The two figures at the centre of the community's life, the priest and the governor, were precisely the offices that oil had marked out.
context.canonical:
The lampstand carries the reader back to the tabernacle. Exodus 25:31 to 37 describes a lampstand of pure, hammered gold with seven lamps, and Exodus 27:20 and 27:21 sets out that the lamps were to be fed with pure oil of pressed olives, and that Aaron and his sons were to tend them from evening until morning. The detail is important. In the tabernacle, human hands trimmed and refilled the lamps. In Zechariah's vision there is no priest at the lampstand; the oil flows from the olive trees through the pipes without any hands at all.

The link between the Spirit and the building of God's house is old. Bezalel was 'filled with the Spirit of God' to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3), and Haggai had told Zerubbabel, 'My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid' (Haggai 2:5). The same principle of dependence appears in Gideon's story, where the LORD pared down the army because Israel might otherwise say, 'My own hand has saved me' (Judges 7:2).

The New Testament carries the images forward. Jesus is anointed 'with the Holy Spirit and with power' (Acts 10:38). He promises His disciples power when the Spirit comes (Acts 1:8). Revelation 1:20 says the seven lampstands are the seven churches, and Revelation 4:5 identifies the seven torches before the throne as the seven Spirits of God. Revelation 11:3 and 11:4 calls the two witnesses 'the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth,' directly taking up Zechariah 4:14. The capstone belongs with the stone of Psalm 118:22, which Jesus applies to Himself (Mark 12:10 and 12:11) and the apostles to His rejection and exaltation (Acts 4:11).

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah meant to speak to a particular discouragement, which was the sense that the work was too big and the workers too few. The comparison with Solomon's temple, the memory of years lost to opposition, and the visible poverty of the community all pressed on the governor and the builders. The vision does not deny the size of the obstacles. It reclassifies them: the great mountain is real, but it stands 'before Zerubbabel,' and in front of the LORD's Spirit it is nothing.

The deeper correction concerns where strength comes from. The word of verse 6 is not a rebuke of effort. Verse 9 says that Zerubbabel's own hands will finish the house. What is rejected is the idea that human might, human numbers or human force would be the source. The lamp that burns without a priest tending it is a deliberate picture of that: the work will be sustained by a supply that is not theirs.

The author also meant to give them permission to be glad of a small start. Verse 10 asks who has despised the day of small things, and the answer is implicitly those who sat and wept at the foundation. The LORD's eyes, which scan the whole earth, take their delight in the sight of the plumb line in Zerubbabel's hand. Whatever the crowd thought, God was already rejoicing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The vision describes how God will carry out a particular work through a particular man, so it should not be read as a promise that every project will succeed or that every mountain will move on request. Zerubbabel was given a word about the temple; Jesus' saying about faith and mountains (Matthew 17:20 and 21:21) is a separate teaching and should not be merged with it.

What carries over is the principle that God's work is sustained by God's Spirit, and that human effort is the instrument and not the source. It is a corrective to activism that trusts programmes, and to passivity that waits for something to happen without doing anything. The text asks for both: Zerubbabel's hands are on the plumb line, and the oil comes from outside.

The word about small things is a pastoral comfort, not a measure of success. It says that God does not despise a modest start. It does not say that small is better, or that numbers never matter.

debates.question: Who are the two olive trees, the two anointed ones?

views.label: Joshua the priest and Zerubbabel the governor
views.case: The two anointed offices of the restoration, priest and king, standing beside the Lord of all the earth and channeling God's grace to the people, matching the fourth and fifth visions and the two men to whom Haggai and Zechariah addressed their words.

views.label: The anointed offices in general, fulfilled in Christ and His witnesses
views.case: The picture of two oil-filled channels points beyond the two men to the offices themselves, taken up in Revelation 11 as God's two witnesses and united finally in Christ the priest-king.

debates.bearing: Either way the point is that God channels His Spirit to His people through His anointed servants, a role that converges in Christ, the fully anointed one.

debates.question: What is the capstone brought forth with shouts of 'Grace, grace'?

views.label: The final top stone of the completed temple
views.case: Zerubbabel will bring out the last stone to finish the house, and the people will shout 'Grace, grace,' acknowledging that God's favor, not their strength, completed it.

views.label: A messianic pointer to the rejected stone made cornerstone
views.case: The prominent stone crowned with shouts of grace anticipates Christ, the stone the builders rejected who became the chief cornerstone, on whom the true temple is built.

debates.bearing: Both readings honor the same truth: the completion of God's house is a work of grace to be shouted over, and it finds its fullness in Christ the cornerstone.

debates.question: Who rejoices at the plumb line in verse 10, and what is it?

views.label: The seven eyes of the LORD rejoice
views.case: The BSB takes the seven eyes, which scan the whole earth, as the subject: God's own sight delights when it sees the plumb line in Zerubbabel's hand. This fits 2 Chronicles 16:9, where the eyes of the LORD roam over the earth to strengthen those whose hearts are fully His.

views.label: Those who despised the small beginning rejoice
views.case: The Hebrew word order allows a different reading, in which those who looked down on the day of small things will rejoice when they see the plumb line, and 'these seven' simply describes the eyes of the LORD. The BSB footnote also notes that the plumb line may be rendered 'the chosen capstone.'

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the eyes of the LORD in view and both celebrate the work of Zerubbabel as the sign that the temple will be finished. The grammar leaves open whether the delight belongs to God alone or is shared by the people who doubted.

study.originalLanguages:
Because the basic level covers the main words, these notes concern some further details of the Hebrew.

Verse 2 describes the lampstand as having a gullah, a 'bowl' at the top. Exodus gives the tabernacle lampstand cups shaped like almond blossoms but no central reservoir, so the bowl is a new feature in this vision: it is the oil tank that makes continuous feeding possible. The next phrase, 'seven spouts to the lamps,' is literally 'seven and seven,' and translators are not agreed whether it means seven channels in all or seven to each lamp. Either way the lamps are fed by many channels, and none of them is a human hand.

In verse 12 the BSB has 'two olive branches beside the two gold pipes from which the golden oil pours.' The BSB footnote says the Hebrew reads 'from which the gold,' so the oil is called simply 'the gold,' and the BSB has supplied 'oil.' This is a striking identification, since the lampstand is gold, the pipes are gold, and the oil is gold; the whole system is of one substance. The word for the 'branches' is shibbole, which is used elsewhere for an ear of grain and for a flowing stream, a double sense that suits olive clusters laden with fruit and oil pouring down.

In verse 7 the words 'Grace, grace to it' are chen chen. Chen means favour or grace, and the repeated word works as an emphasis, as in other repeated cries of Scripture. The 'capstone' is the stone of the 'head,' from the word rosh, and Psalm 118:22 uses the related phrase 'head of the corner' for the rejected stone that became the cornerstone. The BSB footnote on verse 10 adds that the 'plumb line' may be translated 'the chosen capstone,' which shows how tightly the stone and the builder's tool are bound in the verse.

The 'seven eyes of the LORD' in verse 10 'scan the whole earth.' The verb is the one that 2 Chronicles 16:9 uses in the phrase 'the eyes of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth.' It is the verb of a watchman on patrol. God's seeing is active and attentive, and it is aimed at 'those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him.'

Finally, the 'two anointed ones' are standing 'beside the Lord of all the earth.' The Hebrew verb is simply 'stand,' the stance of an attendant before a master. The title 'Lord of all the earth' is an old one; it is the title under which the ark of the covenant goes ahead of Israel into the Jordan (Joshua 3:11 and 3:13). To apply it to the LORD in the midst of an obscure temple project is to assert that this small building belongs to the God who rules the whole earth.

typology.type: The lampstand fed by oil from the trees, Zechariah 4:2 and 4:3
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle lampstand needed Aaron's sons to tend it every evening (Exodus 27:21). The vision removes the priest and shows a lamp that supplies itself from the trees. In Revelation the lampstands are the seven churches, with One like the Son of Man walking among them (Revelation 1:13 and 1:20), and the burning torches before the throne are the seven Spirits of God (Revelation 4:5). Jesus said, 'You are the light of the world' (Matthew 5:14). The type falls short in that a church can lose its lampstand (Revelation 2:5).

typology.type: Zerubbabel's hands finishing the house, Zechariah 4:9
typology.fulfillment: Zerubbabel laid the foundation and finished the house. Zechariah 6:12 and 6:13 say the Branch will 'build the temple of the LORD.' Jesus says, 'I will build My church' (Matthew 16:18), and He speaks of the temple of His body being raised in three days (John 2:19 to 21). Hebrews says Christ is worthy of greater glory than Moses 'just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself' (Hebrews 3:3). The type falls short because Zerubbabel's temple was finite, while the house Christ builds will not fail.

typology.type: The capstone and the cry of grace, Zechariah 4:7
typology.fulfillment: The stone brought out with shouts of 'Grace, grace' meets the stone of Psalm 118:22, which Jesus applied to Himself (Mark 12:10 and 12:11). Peter and Paul describe the church as a building with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20 to 22; 1 Peter 2:4 to 6). John takes up the cry: 'From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace' (John 1:16). The correspondence is partly an echo, and Zechariah's stone is most likely the final stone of the temple, but the New Testament's use of the same image is plain.

Oil marked priests and kings (Exodus 29:7; 1 Samuel 16:13). In Zechariah the offices are held by two men, and Zechariah 6:13 looks ahead to the Branch who 'will be a priest on His throne.' Jesus is the Anointed One, the Christ: 'the Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me' (Luke 4:18). The escalation is that both offices meet in one person, and the Spirit is given to Him 'without limit' (John 3:34). The type falls short in that Joshua and Zerubbabel were two men, each with his own limits.

study.christ:
The word 'Christ' means 'Anointed One,' and Zechariah 4 is a vision about two anointed ones standing beside the Lord of all the earth. The priest and the governor are the two offices the oil marked out, and the Old Testament never gives both to one man on the throne. The hope of the book is that the Branch will be 'a priest on His throne' with 'peaceful counsel between the two' (Zechariah 6:13). Jesus holds both. Psalm 110:4 swears a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, and He sits as King at the right hand of God. In Him the two channels become one.

The Spirit's supply is the second link. The lamp in the vision is fed with no human effort, and John says of Jesus that 'God gives the Spirit without limit' (John 3:34). Isaiah foretold that the Spirit of the LORD would rest on the Branch, the Spirit of wisdom, counsel and strength (Isaiah 11:2). Jesus read Isaiah 61 in the synagogue and said it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18). Peter summarised His ministry as God anointing Him 'with the Holy Spirit and with power' (Acts 10:38). He is the lampstand's full supply. And He pours it out: John records that the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7:39).

Third, the principle of Zechariah 4:6 is the shape of His kingdom. Before Pilate Jesus said, 'My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight' (John 18:36). The King who wins by dying is the definitive case of a work done not by might nor by power. His beginnings were as small as the day of small things: a manger because there was no room, and a servant with 'no stately form or majesty' (Luke 2:7; Isaiah 53:2). He compared His kingdom to a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds that grows into the largest of garden plants (Matthew 13:31 and 13:32).

Fourth, He is the builder of the true temple. Zerubbabel laid the foundation and finished the house, and the Branch of chapter 6 will build the temple of the LORD. Jesus said He would build His church (Matthew 16:18), and He called His own body a temple that would be raised in three days (John 2:19 to 21). Ephesians describes the church as a temple with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20 to 22). And when Paul warns the Galatians, 'After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?' (Galatians 3:3), he is applying Zechariah's principle to the church's life. He who began a good work will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6), which is the confidence Zerubbabel was given about the temple.

A caution applies. The two olive trees of verse 14 are identified in the text as anointed ones standing before the LORD, and the New Testament uses them in Revelation 11 for witnesses, not for Jesus Himself. The link to Christ here goes by way of the offices and the Spirit, not by treating each tree or pipe as a code.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who does His work by supplying it. The lampstand has no wick-trimmer and no oil-bearer; the oil is simply there, flowing from a source the lampstand does not control. That is how the vision pictures divine action. God is not an assistant who steps in when human strength fails. He is the origin of the strength that makes the work possible, and the Spirit through whom He acts is called 'My Spirit,' His own personal presence, not an impersonal force.

He is sovereign over obstacles. The question put to the mountain, 'What are you, O great mountain?', is the talk of one who is not impressed. Before Zerubbabel it will become a plain. The same God is called 'the Lord of all the earth,' a title that makes the temple project a matter of cosmic government, and the empire that stood over Judah a thing under His hand.

He is attentive. The seven eyes scan the whole earth, and they are said to rejoice at the sight of a plumb line in the hand of a builder. This is a God who notices the small, and who takes delight in work that others might dismiss. 2 Chronicles 16:9 says His eyes roam to strengthen those whose hearts are fully His. The people who wept over the foundation thought the thing was too little. God had been watching it from the start.

He works through human hands without handing over His glory. Verse 9 says Zerubbabel's hands will complete the house, and verse 6 says it will not be by might. These are held together without strain. Paul sets the same pairing side by side: 'work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you' (Philippians 2:12 and 2:13). Human labour is real and God's gift makes it so.

He is patient with His prophet. Zechariah is asked twice, 'Do you not know what these are?' and says twice that he does not. The angel does not rebuke him; he explains. God is gracious with a servant who admits what he does not understand.

The passage shapes worship in two ways. It teaches dependence, since a church or a worker can have the appearance of strength and still be without oil. And it gives grace the last word, for the shouts as the capstone is set are 'Grace, grace to it!', not praise of the builder. The glory is the LORD's; the joy is the people's.

crossReferences.note: Haggai asks who remembers the first house and says it must look like nothing by comparison, then tells Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people to be strong and work, because the LORD is with them and His Spirit remains among them. It is the same message as Zechariah 4:6, delivered by the other prophet in the same months.

At the foundation-laying, the people's shouts of joy and the wailing of the old men who had seen the first temple were so mingled that no one could tell them apart. This is the scene behind the question about despising the day of small things, because the weeping and the shouting were both real.

The tabernacle lamps burned pure oil of pressed olives, and Aaron and his sons tended them from evening to morning. Zechariah's lampstand has the same oil but no tending hands, which is how the vision tells Zerubbabel that the supply will not depend on human service.

'The eyes of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him.' It explains the seven eyes of Zechariah 4:10 and tells us who is the object of their search.

The LORD reduces Gideon's army so that Israel cannot say, 'My own hand has saved me.' The reason matches Zechariah 4:6: God sometimes works through weakness so that no one can claim the credit for what he has done.

The temple was completed on the third day of Adar in the sixth year of Darius. This is the check on the promise of verse 9 that Zerubbabel's hands would finish what they began, and it shows the mountain levelled within about four years of the vision.

'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.' The psalm provides the language for a stone brought out with shouts, and the New Testament applies it to Jesus in His rejection and exaltation, which is why the capstone of Zechariah 4:7 is read with Christ in view.

John sees seven golden lampstands with One like the Son of Man among them. In verse 20 they are the churches. The tabernacle lampstand of Zechariah becomes a company of churches, with the risen Christ in the midst of them.

Seven torches of fire burn before the throne, and they are the seven Spirits of God. The seven lamps of Zechariah 4:2 and the seven eyes of 4:10 both appear here as the Spirit's perfect presence before the throne.

The two witnesses are 'the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.' John uses Zechariah's two anointed ones to describe the church's prophetic witness in the last days, so the image continues past its first fulfilment.

Jesus says, 'You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses.' It sets Zechariah 4:6 on the church's doorstep, since the disciples are sent out with no army and no might but the Spirit's power.

God 'who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.' Paul states of believers what Zechariah 4:9 says of the temple, that the hands which began will see the work finished because God is behind it.

The kingdom is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which grows into the largest of garden plants. Jesus describes the same reversal as the day of small things, a modest beginning that no one should despise because of what God will make of it.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is about God dwelling among a people and filling His house with His presence, and again and again the building of that house is shown to depend on His Spirit. Bezalel is filled with the Spirit to make the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3). Solomon builds a temple that heaven cannot contain. When the house is destroyed and the people exiled, the question is whether a battered remnant can rebuild what once stood. Zechariah 4 answers it for the second temple, and in doing so it speaks to every later stage of God's building project.

The vision stands at the point where the story has lost its great visible things. There is no king on the throne and no army, only a governor in a Persian province and a hole in the ground where a temple should be. God's reply is to promise nothing impressive in human terms: not a larger army, a richer treasury, or a friendly emperor. He promises the Spirit, and the finishing of the stone. The story of Scripture repeatedly goes this way. A barren couple, a shepherd boy, a slave in Egypt, a baby in a manger, and a handful of disciples are the means by which the Lord does what could not be done by might or power.

What the vision sets up is the coming of the fully anointed One and the outpouring of His Spirit. The two channels, priest and king, are reunited in Jesus. The Spirit who was in the lampstand's oil is given to all who believe, as Jesus promised (John 7:37 to 39), and at Pentecost the lamp is lit in a community that has no might to speak of. The church becomes the lampstand among whom Christ walks, and the temple built on Christ the cornerstone.

The story ends with the finished house. In the new creation there is no temple, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, and the glory of God gives the city its light, so that the lamp is no longer needed (Revelation 21:22 and 21:23). The shout of 'Grace, grace' that went up over a capstone in Jerusalem becomes the song of the redeemed, who know that the whole thing, from the first stone to the last, was given. The mountain is levelled, the work is done, and the One who began it has carried it to completion.

quiz.q: What is the central message of the vision, spoken to Zerubbabel?

options.text: Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts.
options.note: Verse 6 is the heart of the vision and the motto of the book.

options.text: By hard work and clever strategy the temple will rise.
options.note: Human effort has its place, but the vision credits the Spirit, not might or power.

options.text: Only a great army can accomplish God's purposes.
options.note: The vision explicitly denies that God's work depends on chayil, might or army.

options.text: The temple will never be finished.
options.note: God promises Zerubbabel's hands will complete the house.

quiz.q: What does the self-feeding lampstand picture?

options.text: A work sustained entirely by God's own supply, needing no human hand to fuel it.
options.note: The oil flows from the olive trees automatically, picturing God's continual provision.

options.text: A lamp that will soon burn out for lack of oil.
options.note: The point is the opposite: it never runs dry because God supplies it.

options.text: The need for priests to constantly refill the lamps.
options.note: This lamp is fed without human effort, unlike the ordinary temple lamp.

options.text: The wealth of the Persian Empire.
options.note: The lampstand pictures God's Spirit-supply to His people, not imperial riches.

quiz.q: How does God regard the day of small things?

options.text: He does not despise it; His all-seeing eyes rejoice over a small, faithful beginning.
options.note: Verse 10 shows God delighting in the plumb line in Zerubbabel's hand.

options.text: He is disappointed by anything that starts small.
options.note: The opposite: God rejoices over the small beginning, not despises it.

options.text: He ignores small works until they become large.
options.note: God's eyes actively rejoice over the small start, not ignore it.

options.text: He values only the finished, impressive result.
options.note: He honors the faithful beginning as well as the completion.

quiz.q: How do the two anointed ones point to Christ?

options.text: The offices of priest and king, divided between Joshua and Zerubbabel, are united in Jesus the priest-king.
options.note: Christ alone fully unites both anointed offices, filled with the Spirit without measure.

options.text: They show that Christ holds no office at all.
options.note: The offices point to Christ, who holds both priesthood and kingship.

options.text: They prove there will always be two separate messiahs.
options.note: The two offices converge in the one Christ, not two messiahs.

options.text: They have no connection to Christ.
options.note: The anointed offices of priest and king are fulfilled in Christ.

quiz.q: What is shouted when the capstone is brought forth?

options.text: Grace, grace to it, crediting the completion of God's house to His favor.
options.note: Verse 7 shows the finishing of the temple met with shouts of grace.

options.text: Might and power to the builders.
options.note: The shout is grace, deliberately opposite to might and power.

options.text: Glory to Zerubbabel alone.
options.note: The credit goes to God's grace, not to the governor's achievement.

options.text: Nothing; the work ends in silence.
options.note: The completion is met with joyful shouts of grace.

questions: God's work is done not by might nor by power, but by His Spirit. Where are you relying on your own strength for something only God's Spirit can accomplish?
The lampstand burned by a supply it did not produce. How would it change your week to depend on the Spirit's continual supply rather than your own reserves?
God does not despise the day of small things but rejoices over faithful beginnings. What small, unimpressive act of obedience might God be delighting in right now?
Every mountain of opposition flattens before God's Spirit. What mountain feels immovable to you, and what would it mean to trust God to level it?
The finished house was met with shouts of Grace, grace. How can you make sure God's grace, not your effort, gets the credit for the good in your life?

translationNotes.note: Might renders chayil, the massed strength of an army or nation; power renders koach, the personal strength of an individual; Spirit renders ruach, the divine breath and power of God. The pairing rules out every kind of human strength.

The day of small things names the modest, unimpressive beginning of the temple work; the seven eyes of the LORD that scan the whole earth link to the stone with seven eyes in 3:9, picturing God's full and watchful sight.
Anointed ones renders, literally, the two sons of fresh oil, yitshar; a footnote records the Hebrew and the link to Revelation 11:4, the two witnesses as olive trees and lampstands.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Zechariah 4:1-14. All 14 verses reproduced in order.
